what_it_does: FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays) are reconfigurable chips that let engineers implement custom hardware circuits without fabricating a new chip; very large designs may spread across multiple FPGA chips connected by high-speed links, forming a multi-FPGA system. Within a single large FPGA or between chips, signals travel on long wires called super long lines (SLLs) that cross die boundaries — these introduce significant delay and can create routing bottlenecks. This paper tackles the routing problem (deciding which wire paths signals take) in systems where the inter-chip links are shared in time slices, called time-division multiplexing (TDM), so that many logical signals share the same physical wire by taking turns. The proposed router jointly decides both the physical routing paths and the timing ratios — how much of each time slice each signal gets — rather than solving these two problems separately, reducing critical-path delay and congestion. Quantitative improvements over existing routers should be confirmed in the full paper.
